title: What is the LMAX Disruptor? Explain the lock-free ring buffer, sequences and sequence barriers, the single-writer principle, and why it achieves millions of events per second without the overhead of a BlockingQueue.

s1_definition.profdef: The LMAX Disruptor is a high-performance inter-thread messaging library built around a pre-allocated ring buffer. Producers claim a slot by incrementing a sequence, write their event into the pre-allocated slot in place, and publish the sequence; consumers follow behind using their own sequences and wait on sequence barriers until the data is available. It is lock-free, using compare-and-swap on sequences instead of locks, avoids garbage by reusing slot objects, and is cache-friendly by padding sequences to avoid false sharing. These properties let it process millions of events per second with far lower and more predictable latency than a BlockingQueue, which suffers from lock contention, cache-line bouncing, and per-element allocation.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture a circular conveyor belt at National Bank of India with a fixed number of trays that go round and round. When a trade order arrives, the producer drops the details into the next empty tray (never creating a new tray, just reusing one). Several processing stations downstream—risk check, journaling, matching—follow the belt, each knowing exactly how far ahead it may safely read by watching counters rather than fighting over a shared lock. Because the trays are pre-made and nobody takes turns through a single door, the belt runs blisteringly fast.
s1_definition.oneliner: The Disruptor is a lock-free, pre-allocated ring buffer coordinated by sequences and barriers under a single-writer rule, giving millions of events per second without BlockingQueue lock and allocation overhead.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The LMAX Disruptor is a high-performance inter-thread messaging library built around a pre-allocated ring buffer. Producers claim a slot by incrementing a sequence, write their event into the pre-allocated slot in place, and publish the sequence; consumers follow behind using their own sequences and wait on sequence barriers until the data is available. It is lock-free, using compare-and-swap on sequences instead of locks, avoids garbage by reusing slot objects, and is cache-friendly by padding sequences to avoid false sharing. These properties let it process millions of events per second with far lower and more predictable latency than a BlockingQueue, which suffers from lock contention, cache-line bouncing, and per-element allocation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture a circular conveyor belt at National Bank of India with a fixed number of trays that go round and round. When a trade order arrives, the producer drops the details into the next empty tray (never creating a new tray, just reusing one). Several processing stations downstream—risk check, journaling, matching—follow the belt, each knowing exactly how far ahead it may safely read by watching counters rather than fighting over a shared lock. Because the trays are pre-made and nobody takes turns through a single door, the belt runs blisteringly fast.

**One line to remember:** The Disruptor is a lock-free, pre-allocated ring buffer coordinated by sequences and barriers under a single-writer rule, giving millions of events per second without BlockingQueue lock and allocation overhead.

sections.s2_technical:
The core is a ring buffer: a fixed-size array whose length is a power of two, allocated once at startup. Each slot holds a reusable event object. Because the size is a power of two, mapping a sequence number to a slot is a cheap bitmask (`sequence & (size - 1)`) instead of a modulo. Reusing slot objects means almost no garbage is created at runtime, which avoids garbage-collection pauses that would otherwise spoil latency.

Coordination is done with sequences, which are monotonically increasing counters, not with locks. A producer claims the next sequence, writes its event into that slot in place, then publishes the sequence to make it visible. Each consumer has its own sequence tracking how far it has processed. Producers use compare-and-swap to claim slots, so there is no mutex. The sequences are padded to occupy a full cache line, which prevents false sharing where two unrelated counters on the same cache line keep invalidating each other across cores.

A sequence barrier is how a consumer waits for work without spinning blindly or locking. The barrier tracks the dependent sequences a consumer must stay behind, for example the producer's published sequence, and exposes a wait strategy. The consumer asks the barrier "how far can I safely read?" and the barrier returns the highest available sequence. Wait strategies trade CPU for latency: a busy-spin strategy gives the lowest latency at full CPU, while a blocking strategy uses a lock and condition for lower CPU at higher latency.

The single-writer principle is central. When only one thread writes to a given piece of data, you eliminate write contention entirely, so no locking is needed on that data and the CPU caches behave optimally. The Disruptor applies this by having a single thread own publication of the sequence, and by letting each consumer own its own sequence. Dependencies between consumers are expressed as a graph: a matching-engine consumer can be made to wait behind a journaling consumer and a replication consumer, so the event is safely persisted before it is acted upon.

A senior-level nuance is why this beats an ArrayBlockingQueue. A blocking queue uses a single lock for both put and take, so producers and consumers contend on the same lock and the lock's state bounces between cores. It also typically allocates or wraps elements, creating garbage. The Disruptor separates concerns with independent sequences, uses CAS instead of locks, pre-allocates and reuses slots, and pads against false sharing, which is why it sustains millions of events per second with tight, predictable latency.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's trading platform must ingest a torrent of market order events and process each through risk validation and journaling before matching, at millions per second, with microsecond-level latency. A BlockingQueue between stages became the bottleneck because producers and consumers fought over one lock and the queue allocated objects, causing garbage-collection pauses. This is exactly what the Disruptor solves — a lock-free, pre-allocated ring buffer with no per-event allocation.

Problem 2 — Journaling must happen before matching acts on an order, so stages need an ordering dependency without locks. This is exactly what sequences and sequence barriers provide — the matching consumer waits behind the journaling consumer's sequence.

The project is an order-processing pipeline. Because LMAX Disruptor is an external library, the demo builds a small educational single-producer, single-consumer ring buffer that mirrors the real design: a power-of-two array of reusable `OrderEvent` slots, a producer that claims and publishes a sequence, and a consumer that follows a sequence barrier. The demo publishes orders for Rajesh and Priya and processes them in order with no locks on the data path.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three orders published to a 1024-slot ring buffer, then drained by a single consumer.

Step 1 — At startup the ring pre-allocates all 1024 `OrderEvent` slots. No further allocation happens on the hot path, so the garbage collector stays quiet.

Step 2 — The producer publishes Rajesh's RELIANCE order. It claims sequence 0, maps it to slot 0 via the bitmask, writes the fields into that reused slot in place, then sets the cursor to 0 to publish it.

Step 3 — The producer publishes Priya's TCS order at sequence 1 (slot 1) and Rajesh's INFY order at sequence 2 (slot 2), each writing in place and advancing the cursor.

Step 4 — The consumer calls `drain`. It reads the sequence barrier (the cursor, now 2) to learn the highest available sequence, then processes sequences 0, 1, 2 in order, matching each order. It never locks; it only compares its own sequence to the barrier.

Step 5 — The consumer's sequence reaches 2, equal to the cursor, so it stops. Three orders were processed in strict FIFO order with no locks and no per-event allocation.

Final output:

```
INFO: Matched order SAV2001 RELIANCE 245050.00
INFO: Matched order CUR3001 TCS 180000.00
INFO: Matched order SAV2001 INFY 95000.00
INFO: Processed 3 orders lock-free
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Pre-allocated ring (size=1024, power of two, reused slots)

   slot: [0][1][2][3]...[1023]  (wraps around)
            ▲
   Producer (single writer)
     claim seq=next → write OrderEvent in place → publish cursor=seq
            │  cursor (published sequence) = sequence barrier
            ▼
   Consumer sequence follows behind cursor:
     available = cursor
     while(consumerSeq < available): process slot[seq & mask]; seq++
            │
            ▼
   FIFO order preserved, NO lock, NO per-event allocation

   vs ArrayBlockingQueue:  put/take share ONE lock → contention,
                           wraps elements → garbage → GC pauses
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Disruptor Ring Buffer Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Ring Buffer: fixed power-of-two array, index = seq&mask │
  │  Single-Writer Principle: one publisher, no write locks  │
  │  Sequence Barrier: consumers gate on dependency seqs     │
  │     WHY: lock-free coordination + ordering dependencies  │
  │  Object Reuse (Flyweight): slots mutated in place        │
  │     WHY: zero per-event allocation → no GC pauses        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: ring stores/sequences; handler does business logic   │
  │  O: new consumer stage = add to barrier graph, no change │
  │  D: producers/consumers depend on sequence abstraction   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │     OrderRingBuffer           │ holds ◆│       OrderEvent          │
  │  - slots: OrderEvent[]        │        │  - accountId, symbol      │
  │  - mask: int (size-1)         │        │  - amount: BigDecimal     │
  │  - cursor: AtomicLong         │        │  + set(...)               │
  │  - consumerSeq: long          │        └──────────────────────────┘
  │  + publish(acct,sym,amt)      │  single writer: claim→write→publish
  │  + drain(handler): int        │  barrier: read up to cursor
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ────────────────────────────

  1. new OrderRingBuffer(1024)      → pre-allocate 1024 slots
  2. publish("SAV2001",...)         → seq=0, slot[0].set(...), cursor=0
  3. publish("CUR3001",...)         → seq=1, slot[1].set(...), cursor=1
  4. drain(handler)
  5.   available = cursor (=1)      → sequence barrier
  6.   process slot[0], slot[1]     → FIFO, lock-free

  Contract for publish():
    Pre:  single writer thread only
    Post: slot written in place; cursor advanced (published)
    Perf: no lock, no allocation; O(1) index via bitmask
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The LMAX Disruptor is a high-performance library for passing messages between threads, built around a pre-allocated ring buffer. The ring buffer is a fixed-size array, sized to a power of two, that is allocated once at startup and whose slots hold reusable event objects. Because the size is a power of two, mapping a sequence number to a slot is a cheap bitmask instead of a modulo, and because the slots are reused and mutated in place, almost no garbage is created at runtime, which keeps garbage-collection pauses from ruining latency.

Coordination is done with sequences rather than locks. A sequence is just a monotonically increasing counter. The producer claims the next sequence, writes its event into that slot in place, and publishes the sequence to make it visible. Each consumer has its own sequence and follows behind using a sequence barrier, which tells it the highest sequence it may safely read. The sequences are padded to a full cache line so two unrelated counters do not keep invalidating each other across cores, which is a problem called false sharing. The wait strategy on the barrier lets me trade CPU for latency, from a busy-spin that gives the lowest latency at full CPU to a blocking strategy that uses less CPU at higher latency.

The single-writer principle is the heart of it. When only one thread writes to a given piece of data, there is no write contention at all, so no locking is needed and the CPU caches behave optimally. The Disruptor applies this by having a single publisher advance the sequence and by giving each consumer its own sequence, and it expresses ordering between stages as a dependency graph, so a matching consumer can be made to wait behind a journaling and a replication consumer. This is why it beats an ArrayBlockingQueue, which uses one lock shared by put and take so producers and consumers contend and the lock state bounces between cores, and which also allocates per element and creates garbage.

At National Bank of India our trading platform ingests a torrent of order events that must pass through risk validation and journaling before matching, at millions per second with microsecond latency. A blocking queue between stages became the bottleneck because of lock contention and garbage-collection pauses from per-event allocation. We moved to the Disruptor's ring buffer so the producer publishes into pre-allocated slots with no allocation, consumers follow sequence barriers with no locks, and matching is made to wait behind journaling and replication through the barrier dependency graph, so an order is durably recorded before it is ever acted upon. The sentence I give interviewers is that the Disruptor is a lock-free, pre-allocated ring buffer coordinated by sequences and barriers under a single-writer rule, which is how it reaches millions of events per second with predictable low latency and without the lock and allocation overhead of a BlockingQueue.
